[69] The panel finds that the associated claimant has rebutted the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence that the Haitian state would be unwilling or unable to provide her with adequate protection.

[70] In a general sense, the evidence before the panel is that the Haitian authorities do not have the capacity or the resources to protect persons like the associated claimant from persecution. A report from the Office français de protection des réfugiés et des apatrides makes the following statement (in French) :
" La police peut sembler souvent démunie face à la délinquance armée. Parfois, la police a peur d'intervenir, car les bandits ont des armes. L'équipement de la police peut être inadéquat. Par exemple, lorsque des policiers sont postés le long d'une route, des bandits peuvent attaquer les véhicules qui circulent entre deux groupes de policiers. Ces derniers n'interviennent alors pas. "
" L'insécurité touche tout le monde, y compris les policiers, les magistrats, les avocats, les personnes qui sortent d'une banque, etc. De nombreux policiers sont tués en service par des personnes qui leur volent leurs armes. Il n'existe pas de système de protection des juges, des policiers et des témoins. Parfois, des bandits arrêtés ont des armes " légalisées ", y compris des pistolets de la police.23 "

[71] Moreover, in the associated claimant's personal circumstances, as a person who can barely speak creole, the claimant's ability to access what unlikely state protection might be available to her would be almost completely compromised.

[72] For all of these reasons the associated claimant has rebutted the presumption of state protection.

[80] Having considered all of the evidence, including the testimony of both adult claimants, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX XXXX does not face a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to her life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the United States.

[81] The panel, therefore, finds that she is neither a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act or a person in need or protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act.

[82] The panel, therefore, rejects her claim.

[83] Having considered all of the evidence, including the testimony of both adult claimants, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX does not face a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to his life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture in Haiti.

[84] The panel, therefore, finds that he is not Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act nor a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the Act.

REASONS FOR DECISION
INTRODUCTION

[1] This is the decision of the Refugee Protection Division (the panel) in the claims for refugee protection of XXXX XXXX and his wife XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Haiti, and of their daughter, XXXX XXXX XXXX, a citizen of the United States. They claim refugee protection in Canada pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1
[2] Prior to the start of the hearing, Ms. XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX was named as the designated representative for her daughter, the minor claimant.

[3] The proceedings for this hearing were conducted in English with Haitian Creole interpretation at the request of the claimants and their counsel. Counsel for the claimants provided submissions at the conclusion of the hearing in French. As the hearing was conducted in English, this decision has been written in English.
DETERMINATIONS

[4] The panel finds that XXXX XXXX XXXX does not face a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to her life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the United States.
[5] The panel finds that XXXX XXXX does not face a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to his life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in Haiti.

[6] The panel, therefore, finds that they are not Convention refugees pursuant to section 96 of the Act, nor persons in need of protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act. The panel, therefore, rejects their claims.

[7] The panel finds that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX faces a serious possibility of persecution in Haiti on the basis of her perceived nationality as an American (United States). The panel, therefore, finds that she is a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act. The panel, therefore, accepts her claim.

[8] The panel's reasons are as follows:
ALLEGATIONS
[9] The claimants' detailed allegations are contained in their Basis of Claim Forms (BOCs), including significant amendments made to all BOCs prior to the start of the hearing.2

[10] The claimants' original BOCs were signed on 24 July 2017, XXXX XXXX after they made their refugee claims at the Canada-United States border. In the original BOCs, both adult claimants alleged that they have no fear of returning to Haiti, that they have never had any problems in Haiti, and that the reason they came to Canada was to seek better education and health care for them and for their child. The principal claimant also alleges in his original BOC that he had never made a refugee claim prior to coming to Canada and that the reason he left Haiti in 2008 was to seek education and work opportunities abroad.3

[11] Both adult claimants made substantial amendments to their original BOCs which were signed on 21 August 2017. These amendments fundamentally contradicted the statements made by the claimants in their original BOCs.

[12] According to his new BOC4, the principal claimant fears serious harm or death in Haiti by the Lavalas political party. Beginning in XXXX 2006, the claimant allegedly found out that he was on a Lavalas party political enemies list. The claimant was allegedly on this list because he had made negative comments concerning the Lavalas party in the course of his work as a XXXX.
[13] This led to numerous incidents of threats and violence by the Lavalas party members against the claimant.

[14] In XXXX 2008, after a previous failed attempt, the claimant left Haiti for the United States. The claimant made an asylum claim in the United States. That claim was based on essentially the same allegations as are contained in the claimant's Canadian refugee claim. The claim in the United States was rejected.

[15] In her amended BOC5, the associated claimant alleges that she fears returning to Haiti because she has lived almost her entire life in the United States, she barely speaks creole and when she does, it is with an American accent, and as a result she would be particularly vulnerable to kidnapping for ransom and other violent crimes.
[16] At the hearing, the principal claimant alleged that he fears the minor claimant returning to the United States, because in returning to the United States she would be separated from her family.

[17] All claimants came to Canada from the United States on XXXX XXXX 2017, making refugee claims at the Canada-United States border.
ANALYSIS
Identity

[18] The adult claimants' personal and national identities as citizens of Haiti, are established on a balance of probabilities by their testimony and by the documentary evidence on file, including certified copies of their Haitian passports.6

[19] The minor claimant's personal and national identity as a citizen of the United States is established on a balance of probabilities by a certified copy of her American passport, also on file.7
MINOR CLAIMANT

[20] The panel finds that the minor claimant has failed to establish that she faces a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to her life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the United States.
[21] At the hearing, the principal claimant alleged that the minor claimant faces a risk in returning to the United States, because she would be separated from her family.

[22] On this issue, the Act does not provide the panel with jurisdiction to make decisions on the basis of humanitarian and compassionate considerations. Moreover, the Federal Court of Canada has held that family separation does not amount to persecution, a personal risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or to a danger of torture in the Canadian refugee law.8 Canadian jurisprudence recognizes the general right of countries to regulate and control the granting of citizenship and the entry of non-nationals into their territory9. It follows that the minor claimant's separation from her parents were she to return to the United States, is insufficient to establish her claim under either section 96 or section 97(1) of the Act.

[23] Moreover, given that the associated claimant's claim is being accepted by the panel, it would be speculative to find that, on a balance of probabilities, the minor claimant would be returned to the United States without her parents. The minor claimant has not established that, on a balance of probabilities, this would occur. Indeed, the panel finds that it is more likely than not, that the minor claimant will remain in Canada with her mother pursuant to other provisions of the Act.

[24] The best interests of the minor claimant is a primary concern of the panel in its consideration of her refugee claim. This concern, however, cannot be the basis for accepting her as a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection. This concern for the best interests of children cannot relieve a claimant, even a minor claimant, from establishing their claim according to the requirements of sections 96 or 97(1) of the Act. The concept of family unity does not relieve a refugee claimant from the onus of demonstrating, that he or she falls within the definition of a Convention refugee or a protected person.10

[25] Other than separation from her family, no other allegations have been made by the claimants regarding the minor claimant and a fear of returning to the United States.
PRINCIPAL CLAIMANT

[26] The determinative issue in the principal claimant's claim is credibility. The panel finds that the principal claimant is not credible for the following reasons. This finding is determinative of the panel's analysis of his allegations under both sections 96 and section 97(1) of the Act.
Credibility
Verbal threats
[27] The claimant's allegations were contradictory with respect to the time period between learning about the enemies list in XXXX 2006 and the first attack against him on XXXX XXXX 2007.

[28] In his United States asylum documents, the claimant alleged that:
"At the end of XXXX 2006, a friend who resided in the neighborhood, advised me to take precautions because some members of Lavalas organized a meeting and they had a list with names that they will be maltreated and I was included on that list. In order for me to take care of myself and my family, I was obligated to continue with my daily activity and I was also receiving verbal threats (my emphasis)."11

[29] In the principal claimant's amended BOC, he states that (in French), "Afin de subvenir à mes besoins et à ceux de ma famille, j'étais obligé de poursuivre mes activités quotidiennes malgré les menaces".12 This statement is less precise than the statement made in the United States asylum form. It is unclear in this statement if the claimant is referring to being on the enemies list or to ongoing threats that he was receiving in this period.

[30] At the hearing, the panel asked the claimant if he had any problems with the Lavalas members between XXXX 2006 and the attack on XXXX XXXX 2007. The claimant testified that there were no problems during that time. Asked by the panel to explain why, therefore, he had declared in his United States asylum claim that he received ongoing verbal threats in this period, the claimant explained that he was referring to learning about the existence of the list. The claimant interpreted learning about the list as a threat against him.

[31] The panel does not accept this explanation for the claimant's contradictory testimony as reasonable. The clear meaning of the claimant's statement in the United States asylum claim document is that he was receiving threats in an ongoing manner as he continued to work to support his family. The statement clearly implies multiple verbal threats in the time period after the claimant learned about the list. Moreover, the threats are described as verbal threats. Finding out about his name being on an enemy's list is not a verbal threat. The panel does not, therefore, accept as credible the claimant's explanation that he was referring to learning about the list when he stated that he was receiving ongoing verbal threats.

[32] The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility because of this contradictory testimony.
Omission of efforts to locate the claimant after his departure
[33] The claimant made a significant allegation at the hearing that was not contained in either his United States asylum documents or in his Canadian BOC.

[34] At the hearing, the claimant alleged that once he was in the United States, he was told by his cousin that Lavalas members continued to search for him. According to the claimant's testimony at the hearing, the Lavalas members had stopped the claimant's cousin on the street in Haiti, asking about the claimant's whereabouts. When the cousin told them that the claimant was no longer in Haiti, the Lavalas members allegedly stated that they will continue to search for the claimant even though he was no longer in the country.

[35] Asked by the panel why he did not include this significant information in either his United States or Canadian claim forms, the claimant explained that he did not think it was relevant as he was in the United States when this incident took place.

[36] The panel does not accept this explanation as reasonable. The agents of persecution alleged ongoing interest in the claimant after his departure from Haiti goes to the heart of his claim. In his amended BOC, a document prepared with the assistance of an experienced counsel, the claimant goes so far as to state that he knows that the people who attacked him are still in Haiti. Given this statement, an indication that the claimant had turned his mind to whether the threat in Haiti still existed, and given that the claimant was assisted by a counsel in preparing the amendment, it is reasonable in the circumstances to expect that the claimant would have also provided this important allegation.

[37] The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the claimant's credibility because of this significant omission.
Statements at the border and in original BOC

[38] At the Canada-United States border, both of the adult claimants made nearly identical statements regarding the absence of risk for them in Haiti. The principal claimant told Canadian immigration officials that he has never faced persecution in Haiti and that he was coming to Canada to seek a better life for his family, including health care and education for his child.13

[39] The claimants' repeated these statements in their original BOCs, signed XXXX XXXX after their interview at the border, adding that the principal claimant had left Haiti in 2008 to seek work and education abroad.14

[40] In the amendment to his BOC, the principal claimant explained that the statements made in his original BOC were the result of being afraid of deportation to the United States or to Haiti and fear of being imprisoned. The claimant did not provide an explanation in the amended BOC as to why he had repeated the statements in his original BOC, a form signed XXXX XXXX after his interview at the border.15

[41] At the hearing, the claimant repeated these explanations with respect to the statements he made at the border. Regarding the statements made in his original BOC, a form prepared XXXX XXXX after his interview at the border, the claimant testified that he did not have the guidance of a lawyer in preparing the BOC. He also testified that he believed his uncle would guide him through the process.
[42] The panel does not accept these explanations as reasonable.

[43] The statements made by the claimants at the border are not minor contradictions or inconsistencies with their testimony at the hearing. The claimants went out of their way to tell immigration officials that they have never had any problems in Haiti, that they do not fear persecution in Haiti, and to provide officers with an explanation as to why they are coming to Canada - a better life for their family, including health care and education.

[44] The principal claimant's explanation that he was too afraid to explain the true reasons for coming to Canada is also inconsistent with the fact that the claimant, when pressed by the immigration officer, in fact stated that it was possible he could be kidnapped if he returned to Haiti.16 Given that the claimant went so far as to state that he could be kidnapped in Haiti, an indication that he was willing to make a statement about what possible negative consequences a return to Haiti could have for him, it is reasonable in the circumstances to expect that he would have also stated that he was under an ongoing risk of death from Lavalas party members.

[45] The panel similarly finds that the claimants' explanations for failing to explain the true reasons for their refugee claims in their original BOCs are unreasonable. The principal claimant was unable to explain at the hearing why he needed the guidance of a lawyer in order to state in his original BOC the true reasons that he was making a refugee claim in Canada. The claimant's answers in his BOC clearly indicate that he understood the nature of the questions being asked. The panel also notes that the principal claimant had already made an asylum claim in the United States and was, therefore, familiar with the concept of making a claim for asylum.

[46] The panel draws a negative inference with respect to the principal claimant's credibility, as a result of these fundamental contradictions between his port-of entry-interview, his original BOC, his amended BOC, and his testimony at the hearing.
[47] For all of these reasons the panel finds that the principal claimant is not credible.
[48] The claimants provided no personal documentary evidence in support of the principal claimant's allegations of persecution in Haiti by the Lavalas party members.

[49] For all of these reasons, the panel finds that the principal claimant has failed to establish, on a balance of probabilities, that he was targeted in Haiti by members of the Lavalas political party between 2006 and 2008, nor that he would be targeted by them should he return to Haiti.
Kidnapping

[50] Although in his BOC and at the hearing the principal claimant alleges no other reasons that he fears returning to Haiti, the panel has also considered if he would face a risk of kidnapping, as per the principal claimant's statement to the Canadian immigration officials at the Canada - United States border.17
[51] The panel notes that the claimant speaks fluent Creole, has lived in Haiti as an adult, and has family connections in the country.
[52] The panel finds that the claimant's fear of kidnapping is not linked to any of the five Convention grounds.
[53] The panel also finds that this is a generalized risk faced by all Haitians.

[54] The documentary evidence before the panel is that crime in Haiti, including kidnappings for ransom, robbery, and murder, are unfortunately endemic across all segments of the Haitian population.18 Although persons returning from abroad may be targeted for these sorts of crimes due to a perception that they have money, the panel finds that their targeting does not distinguish them from other Haitians who are similarly targeted and victimized by rampant criminality.

[55] The panel notes that this finding is consistent with the Federal Court reasoning in Prophète with respect to the targeting of Haitians returning from abroad, based on the perception that they have money.19
ASSOCIATED CLAIMANT
Nexus
[56] The panel finds that, on a balance of probabilities, the associated claimant's allegations establish a nexus to the Convention ground of perceived American nationality.

[57] Although the claimant is not a citizen of the United States, there are several factors particular to her that would, on a balance of probabilities, lead her to being perceived as an American were she to return to Haiti. Foremost among these factors is that the associated claimant barely speaks creole and when she does, she speaks with a thick American accent. The panel also notes that the associated claimant left Haiti when she was eight years old, more than twenty-five years ago, has never since returned to Haiti, and has no connections to any family in Haiti. The claimant testified that she has no understanding of the society and culture of Haiti. For all intents and purposes, except in law, the claimant is a de facto American and would, in the panel's view, be perceived as American in Haiti.
Credibility
[58] The panel's previously articulated concerns with respect the principal claimant's statements at the border and in his original BOC also apply to the associated claimant.

[59] However, the associated claimant has additional allegations, separate and distinct from those of her husband, which the panel finds have been credibly established. These are the associated claimant's allegations of being a woman who barely speaks creole, who was brought to the United States as a young child, and who has virtually no personal family connections in Haiti.

[60] On these aspects of her claim, the associated claimant testified in a straight forward, sincere and open manner. There were no relevant inconsistencies, contradictions or omissions that were not reasonably explained.

[61] For example, the panel noted that, according to the notes from the associated claimant's interview with CBSA officers at the border, the interview was conducted with creole interpretation.20 The associated claimant, however, explained that the questions were asked to her in French, that she understood the questions in French, and that she answered in English before the creole interpretation was provided. I find this explanation credible and reasonable. I also note, that the claimant declared at the outset of the hearing that she did not speak creole and would, therefore, require interpretation of the proceedings into English or for the proceedings to take place in English.

[62] Given her credible testimony, the panel finds that the associated claimant has established, on a balance of probabilities, that she has lived most of her life in the United States, that she barely speaks creole, that when she does speak creole it is with a thick American accent, and that she has no family contacts in Haiti.

[63] The panel finds that in the chaotic and dangerous world of contemporary Haiti, the perception that the claimant is American would, coupled with her virtually non-existent personal resources to function in the country, place the claimant in danger of kidnapping for ransom, assaults, and other targeted violent crimes because of her perceived American nationality.21

[64] Although the associated claimant's risk in this sense is connected to the perception that Americans have money, it is the claimant's particular circumstances, as a person who barely speaks creole and who has a very limited understanding of Haitian society that would put her at risk as an easily identifiable perceived American.

[65] The panel notes that the principal claimant's circumstances, although he has lived in the United States for ten years, are materially different from those of his wife. The principal claimant speaks creole fluently, has lived in Haiti as an adult, understands how to function in the Haitian social context, and maintains family connections in the country. The panel finds that the principal claimant would not, on a balance of probabilities, be perceived in Haiti as an American.

[66] The country evidence before the panel establishes that the associated claimant's profile, a profile as an easily identifiable and particularly vulnerable perceived national of the United States, gives rise to a serious possibility of persecution for her in Haiti.

[67] A Response to Information Request in the National Documentation Package for Haiti states the following:
"According to the Director of the Institute for Justice and Democracy in Haiti (IJDH), a Boston-based organization promoting human rights in Haiti, middle-class and affluent Haitians, which may include members of the Haitian diaspora, have a higher individual risk of victimization by criminals in Haiti than do their lower-income counterparts. He explained, in correspondence with the Research Directorate, that Haitians who have lived abroad are perceived to have access to more resources and may therefore be more likely to be targeted by criminals for crimes such as kidnapping for ransom."22

[68] Again, what provides a nexus between this risk and the Convention, what distinguishes the risk faced by the associated claimant and other Haitians who return to Haiti after having lived abroad, are the very particular circumstances of the associated claimant. These factors are the claimant's very limited ability to speak creole, her American accent, her departure from Haiti as a young child, and the resulting perception that she is an American rather than a Haitian who has lived in the United States.
State Protection

[69] The panel finds that the associated claimant has rebutted the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence that the Haitian state would be unwilling or unable to provide her with adequate protection.

[70] In a general sense, the evidence before the panel is that the Haitian authorities do not have the capacity or the resources to protect persons like the associated claimant from persecution. A report from the Office français de protection des réfugiés et des apatrides makes the following statement (in French) :
" La police peut sembler souvent démunie face à la délinquance armée. Parfois, la police a peur d'intervenir, car les bandits ont des armes. L'équipement de la police peut être inadéquat. Par exemple, lorsque des policiers sont postés le long d'une route, des bandits peuvent attaquer les véhicules qui circulent entre deux groupes de policiers. Ces derniers n'interviennent alors pas. "
" L'insécurité touche tout le monde, y compris les policiers, les magistrats, les avocats, les personnes qui sortent d'une banque, etc. De nombreux policiers sont tués en service par des personnes qui leur volent leurs armes. Il n'existe pas de système de protection des juges, des policiers et des témoins. Parfois, des bandits arrêtés ont des armes " légalisées ", y compris des pistolets de la police.23 "

[71] Moreover, in the associated claimant's personal circumstances, as a person who can barely speak creole, the claimant's ability to access what unlikely state protection might be available to her would be almost completely compromised.

[72] For all of these reasons the associated claimant has rebutted the presumption of state protection.
Internal flight alternative

[73] The panel finds that the associated claimant faces a serious possibility of persecution on the basis of her perceived American nationality throughout Haiti. The violent crimes that would very likely be targeted at the associated claimant as a perceived American exists throughout the country, as does the lack of state protection.

[74] Moreover, as a person who does not speak creole and has no family connections in Haiti, any internal flight alternative would be objectively unreasonable in the associated claimant's personal circumstances.

[75] The panel finds that, on a balance of probabilities, there is no viable internal flight alternative for the associated claimant anywhere in Haiti.
CONCLUSION
[76] For all these reasons, the panel finds that the associated claimant has established that she has a subjective fear of return to Haiti that is objectively well-founded.

[77] Having considered all of the evidence, including the testimony of both adult claimants, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX faces a serious possibility of persecution in Haiti on the basis of her perceived nationality as an American (United States).
[78] The panel, therefore, finds that she is a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act.
[79] The panel, therefore, accepts her claim.

[80] Having considered all of the evidence, including the testimony of both adult claimants, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX XXXX does not face a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to her life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture in the United States.
[81] The panel, therefore, finds that she is neither a Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act or a person in need or protection pursuant to section 97(1) of the Act.
[82] The panel, therefore, rejects her claim.

[83] Having considered all of the evidence, including the testimony of both adult claimants, the panel finds that XXXX XXXX does not face a serious possibility of persecution, a personal risk to his life or of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture in Haiti.
[84] The panel, therefore, finds that he is not Convention refugee pursuant to section 96 of the Act nor a person in need of protection pursuant to section 97 of the Act.

[85] The panel, therefore, rejects his claim.
